Week 78 Appendix: The Week the Clock Held Its Breath

Fatal ICE shootings, a war resumed without authorization, and a primetime bid to relitigate 2020 nearly offset each other to a standstill.

This week combined an active foreign military conflict, an unprecedented assault on election legitimacy, and a cascade of law-enforcement lethality that together reveal an executive branch increasingly unconstrained by institutional checks. Trump's refusal to sign bipartisan legislation absent voter-restriction concessions, his circumvention of War Powers Act notice requirements for renewed Iran strikes, and his prime-time address recycling debunked 2020 election fraud claims (backed by DHS threats of criminal prosecution against state election officials) collectively signal deliberate groundwork for contesting future election outcomes. Simultaneously, ICE's expanding, poorly vetted enforcement apparatus produced multiple fatal shootings of non-target civilians within days, prompting a policy reversal driven not by accountability concerns but by MAGA-base pressure. DOJ subpoenas of NYT journalists, judicial sanctioning of a manufactured Trump-IRS settlement, and the sudden firing of a judicially-appointed U.S. attorney reveal a Justice Department alternately weaponized against critics and shielding the president. Death of Senator Graham and rapid family-based succession, alongside emoluments-adjacent stories (Kushner land deals, defense-contract enrichment for Trump's sons), rounded out a week defined by institutional strain across nearly every branch.

Power and Authority

  1. Trump refused to sign a bipartisan housing bill unless Congress passed a voting-restriction measure: The president used his signature power as leverage to force voting restrictions, letting a bipartisan bill become law only through the pocket-veto mechanism. (2026-07-11)
  2. Trump notified Congress of resumed strikes on Iran under a reinterpreted War Powers Act clock: The administration claimed a fresh 60-day window for military action without new congressional authorization, sidestepping constitutional war powers. (2026-07-11)
  3. Trump held a secret Camp David meeting with select House Republicans to build a budget package bypassing Democrats: Excluding moderate members and confiscating phones during closed-door budget talks weakened transparent, inclusive legislative process. (2026-07-11)
  4. Trump posted threats of massive military strikes against Iran on social media: Presidential threats of large-scale destruction, issued informally via social media, escalated tensions without deliberative process. (2026-07-11)
  5. Trump tied renewal of a foreign surveillance law to passage of the voting-restriction Save America Act: Conditioning national security legislation on partisan electoral measures represents coercion of Congress by the executive. (2026-07-13)
  6. Trump ordered airstrikes on Iran and announced a naval blockade of Iranian shipping: Unilateral military escalation, including a blockade equivalent to an act of war, proceeded without apparent congressional authorization. (2026-07-12) [single source]
  7. Trump ousted three members of an independent federal election-administration commission: Removing independent election commissioners ahead of midterms signals executive interference with nonpartisan election oversight. (2026-07-13)
  8. Trump recommended Lindsey Graham's sister for the vacated South Carolina Senate seat, overriding a sitting senator's own preference: The president's direct intervention in a state appointment shows executive influence reaching into supposedly independent state Senate succession decisions. (2026-07-13)
  9. Trump directed the Department of Justice to dismiss seditious conspiracy convictions against Proud Boys leaders: A Trump-appointed judge reluctantly granted the dismissal, acknowledging it was driven by political motive rather than law, undermining accountability for January 6 violence. (2026-07-11)
  10. Trump constructed a helipad on the White House South Lawn without congressional review or zoning process: Building major infrastructure on federal grounds outside statutory review, funded partly by a defense contractor, bypassed legislative and regulatory checks. (2026-07-16)
  11. Trump announced a nationally televised address relitigating the 2020 election with claims of foreign interference: The president used a formal presidential platform to promote debunked election-fraud claims explicitly to pressure passage of voter-restriction legislation. (2026-07-16)
  12. Trump ordered the Department of Homeland Security to direct states to purge noncitizens from voter rolls using a tool federal courts have repeatedly blocked: The directive revives a mechanism courts found unreliable and unconstitutional sixteen times, overriding judicial determinations to pressure state election systems. (2026-07-17) [single source]
  13. Trump demanded Congress pass the SAVE America voter-restriction act, framing refusal as evidence of cheating: Public pressure delegitimizing legislative independence tied election-restriction passage to unsubstantiated accusations against opponents. (2026-07-17) [single source]
  14. Trump fired a judicially appointed U.S. attorney within an hour of his swearing-in: Removing a prosecutor appointed unanimously by federal judges demonstrates executive assertion of unilateral control over supposedly independent law enforcement appointments. (2026-07-17)
  15. Trump administration overturned a DHS memo halting ICE traffic stops after two fatal shootings within days: Executive override of an agency safety pause, driven by political pressure rather than accountability findings, prioritized enforcement volume over documented civilian deaths. (2026-07-15)
